title: Show us the Father (John 14:8–21)
hookLine: Philip asks, and he says: whoever has seen me has seen the Father
last: LET NOT YOUR HEART BE TROUBLED.

cards: Philip is the practical one. Back in chapter six, with a hungry crowd on a hillside, about five thousand men by John's count, Philip did the math: two hundred pennyworth of bread wouldn't be enough.
Now it's the last supper, and Jesus has been talking about going to the Father, about the way, about knowing the Father already. And Philip says the plain thing. Enough talk.
Just show us. One look, and we'll be satisfied. It's a very honest request.

teach.h: SHOW US THE FATHER, AND IT'S ENOUGH.
teach.b: In the King James Bible Philip says: "Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us." That would do it.

teach.h: SO LONG WITH YOU, AND YOU DON'T KNOW ME?
teach.b: The reply comes with a little ache in it: "Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father."
All those meals and roads and boats, and Philip is still waiting for the real thing to show up. The answer is that it already has.
Moses once asked to see God's glory, and in Exodus he is told no one can see God's face and live.

teach.h: NO ONE HAS SEEN GOD; THE SON MAKES HIM KNOWN.
teach.b: In its first chapter, John's Gospel struck the same note: no one has seen God at any time, and the Son has made him known. So when Philip asks to see, the Gospel's answer is a person at a table.
Watch how he washes feet, who he eats with, how he speaks to a grieving sister: John's claim is that this is what God is like. Christians have built a great deal on this line.
Churches that teach the Trinity read it alongside their teaching that the Father and the Son are distinct and yet one God, and theologians have worked long and hard on how to say that well.
Philip wants a vision in the sky.
He's offered a face across the table.

teach.h: HE THAT HATH SEEN ME HATH SEEN THE FATHER.
teach.b: Then Jesus promises he won't leave them orphans: "I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you." Another helper is coming, he says, to stay with them.

how: John 14 is often read at Christian funerals and in the Easter season, and Christians hear in Jesus's reply to Philip a claim at the center of their faith: that in Jesus, God is made known.

s: Philip asks to see the Father at the last supper
he asks at the table: "Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us."
Jesus tells Philip the Father will appear in the sky
he points to himself: "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father."
Jesus promises not to leave his friends comfortless
"I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you."

games.q: you're Philip. Jesus has been talking a long time about the Father. you want something more solid. what do you say?
o: show us the Father, and that'll be enough.
games.why: Philip asks to be shown, and the answer turns him back to the person in front of him: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.

practice: Bring to mind one scene from the Gospels where Jesus is kind, washing the disciples' feet, bending down to write in the dirt, calling a short man down from a tree, and let it play slowly: watch his hands, and who he looks at.
If you're a Christian, this is what the line says God looks like; if you're learning, simply notice what kind of face the Gospel is describing. If you pray, hold that scene before God in silence.

wordCard.voice: Philip. The practical disciple who asked Jesus, show us the Father, and heard that he already had, in Jesus himself.
